title: Nurse-Led Antenatal Care in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Prospective Cohort Study with Difference-in-Differences Analysis.
paragraphs: Fragile and conflict-affected settings face profound health system disruptions, including workforce shortages, fragmented service delivery, and reduced access to essential maternal health services. Task-shifting from physicians to nurses has been promoted as a pragmatic strategy to sustain service delivery; yet, empirical evidence on its impact on biological and neonatal outcomes in active conflict settings remains scarce. The critical question is whether nurse-led care models can function as an adaptive strategy that preserves outcomes during health system collapse.

In Al-Dhalea Governorate, where this study was conducted, access to antenatal care (ANC) is severely constrained. Only 45% of health facilities are fully functional, with physician-to-population ratios of 1:15,000 (far below WHO recommendations) and 2 to 3 nurses per facility serving 5,000 to 10,000 people. Iron-folate supply disruptions occur for 3 to 4 months annually, and referral pathways are often obstructed by road closures. The baseline prevalence of anemia among pregnant women is estimated at 70% to 75%, with food insecurity affecting more than 60% of households.

Maternal anemia remains a critical global challenge, disproportionately affecting low-resource and conflict-affected settings. 1 Defined as hemoglobin levels < 11 g/dL during pregnancy, anemia contributes to preterm birth, low birth weight, and maternal mortality. 2 In humanitarian crises, health systems face compounded challenges: infrastructure collapse, workforce shortages, supply chain disruptions, and displacement. 3 Yemen exemplifies this fragility, with over a decade of conflict leaving an estimated 65% of pregnant women anemic and maternal mortality rates having tripled since 2015. 4 The burden of maternal anemia is not confined to Yemen; recent evidence from other humanitarian settings, such as refugee populations in Uganda, reported an anemia prevalence of 52.6% among pregnant women, with low educational attainment and food insecurity identified as key determinants. 5

Strengthening nurse-delivered ANC through structured protocols, systematic screening, and algorithm-based management has emerged as an essential adaptation. 6 ANC is a promising domain for optimization, given its preventive, protocol-driven nature. 7 While task-shifting has shown effectiveness in HIV and immunization programs, 8 , 9 its impact on maternal anemia and birth outcomes in active conflict settings remains inadequately documented. Previous studies in stable settings suggest that nurse-led interventions can improve ANC attendance and maternal knowledge, 10 but evidence from conflict zones is scarce, with most studies focusing on process rather than biological outcomes. 11 There is still little data on the efficacy of organized, nurse-led treatments in enhancing biological and newborn outcomes in active conflict areas, despite recent research showing the high prevalence of anemia in humanitarian contexts and identifying related risk factors. 5 Instead than focusing on clinical outcomes, the majority of previous research has examined procedural indicators like attendance rates. Therefore, strong prospective evidence is essential for guiding measures to enhance the health system in fragile environments.

We conceptualize nurse-led ANC as de facto nursing leadership that emerges when physicians are structurally constrained. This informal leadership manifests across three dimensions: (1) clinical leadership—independent, protocol-driven anemia management; (2) administrative leadership—coordinating follow-up and referrals despite supply disruptions; and (3) community leadership—sustaining health education and patient engagement. We hypothesize that these dimensions, operationalized through structured protocols, may translate into measurable biological improvements. This framework guides interpretation while acknowledging that leadership was not directly measured but inferred from implementation fidelity.

The theoretical foundation derives from the chronic care model adapted to humanitarian contexts, emphasizing structured follow-up, patient education, and protocol-based management. 12 Complex confounders in fragile environments, such as supply interruptions, security limitations, and varied training, are frequently overlooked in existing studies. 11 New research indicates that health literacy may interact with nursing complexity to influence patient outcomes 13 and that nursing variables may mediate the relationship between patient clinical complexity and organizational outcomes. 14 Therefore, there is an urgent need for solid prospective research about whether improved nurse-led ANC improves biological and neonatal outcomes in active combat zones.

This study addresses these gaps by evaluating a fragility-adapted intervention in Al-Dhalea, Yemen. Specifically, we aimed to: (1) quantify associations between nurse-led ANC and hemoglobin, anemia, and birth outcomes compared to routine ANC; (2) assess whether structured nurse-led ANC demonstrates characteristics consistent with de facto nursing leadership across clinical, administrative, and community dimensions, as measured by implementation fidelity; and (3) derive a preliminary adaptation framework for health system strengthening in degrading contexts while acknowledging observational evidence limitations.

We conducted a prospective cohort study between January and December 2025 across 12 public primary healthcare facilities in Al-Dhalea Governorate, southern Yemen—a region severely affected by protracted conflict, fragmented health services, recurrent displacement, and chronic shortages of medical personnel and supplies. Facilities were purposively selected to represent typical service delivery in conflict-affected settings, including intermittent laboratory functionality, essential medicine stockouts, and limited referral pathways. A comprehensive contextual profile, including facility characteristics, implementation challenges, and adaptive strategies, is available in File S12 .

The 12 facilities comprised six nurse-led and six routine ANC sites, selected based on (1) trained nurse availability, (2) geographic distribution (urban/rural balance), and (3) protocol implementation capacity. Nurse-led facilities had slightly better baseline staffing (mean 2.2 vs 1.3 ANC nurses per facility) and laboratory functionality (83% vs 50% with functional labs) compared to routine facilities. These differences were addressed through facility-level covariate adjustment and sensitivity analyses and are discussed as a key limitation. Detailed facility-level characteristics (staffing, laboratory functionality, power availability, security access, catchment population) are provided in File S12 .

Pregnant women seeking prenatal care at participating facilities during the recruiting period were included in the study population. To reduce selection bias, all eligible women who visited each institution throughout the recruiting period were asked to take part.

Exclusion criteria were known hemoglobinopathies (eg, sickle cell disease, thalassemia), chronic renal impairment, active tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, or any medical condition requiring specialized obstetric care (eg, cardiac disease, pre-existing diabetes). These exclusions were applied to minimize clinical heterogeneity and reduce confounding by underlying pathologies affecting hemoglobin metabolism or pregnancy outcomes.

Nurse-led enhanced ANC cohort: Women who received structured antenatal care delivered primarily by trained nurses following a standardised care protocol detailed in File S6 . The protocol included systematic haemoglobin screening, algorithm-based anaemia management, regular follow-up visits, nutrition education, and clear referral pathways.

The allocation of participants to nurse-led or routine ANC was determined by facility-level implementation capacity rather than individual randomization. The 12 participating facilities were purposively selected to ensure representation of both care models based on (1) the availability of trained nurses for the enhanced protocol and (2) geographic distribution to include comparable urban/rural settings. Women received the type of ANC available at the facility where they enrolled. To minimize selection bias, all eligible women presenting to each facility during the recruitment period were invited to participate, and baseline characteristics were rigorously measured and adjusted for in the analyses.

The sample size was estimated to detect a clinically meaningful difference in mean hemoglobin concentration between groups. Based on pilot data from similar settings in Yemen, we assumed a mean difference of 0.5 g/dL with a standard deviation of 1.2 g/dL. With α = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power, the required sample size was 91 participants per group. Accounting for a 15% loss to follow-up, we targeted 107 participants per group (214 total). For increased precision and to accommodate subgroup analyses, we recruited 225 participants per group (450 total). Detailed power calculation methodology and assumptions are provided in File S9 .

Data were collected using structured, pre-tested instruments ( File S4 ). At enrollment, trained data collectors (midwives with ≥ 2 years of experience, see File S5 for training details) administered baseline questionnaires capturing socio-demographic characteristics, obstetric history, gestational age, and baseline hemoglobin levels measured using HemoCue ® Hb 301 devices. Follow-up assessments occurred during scheduled ANC visits and at delivery, with hemoglobin remeasured at 32–34 weeks. Birth outcomes were abstracted from facility records or obtained through structured postnatal interviews for community births. All data collectors underwent standardized training ( File S5 ), and data management followed a predefined protocol ( File S8 ). A single quantitative item (scale 1–10) was used to evaluate patient satisfaction as a secondary process measure. The SRQR and COREQ checklists mentioned in the supplemental files apply to the systematic documenting of implementation fidelity and process indicators rather than formal qualitative research components because we did not gather qualitative interview data.

Based on directed acyclic graphs constructed a priori, we distinguished between confounders (variables affecting both exposure and outcome) and mediators (variables on the causal pathway). The following covariates were identified for adjustment in the main models as potential confounders:

The following variables were considered potential mediators rather than confounders and were therefore not included as adjustment variables in the primary models: (1) the number of ANC visits and (2) adherence to iron–folic acid supplementation. These variables were instead analyzed separately in a mediation analysis to quantify the pathways through which the intervention may have operated (see the Mediation Analysis section and Figure S2 ).

Baseline characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics: means (SD) or medians (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies (percentages) for categorical variables. Group differences were assessed using Student’s t -test or Mann–Whitney U -test for continuous variables, and χ 2 or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables.

Multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors estimated the adjusted association between nurse-led ANC and follow-up hemoglobin. Multivariable logistic regression was used for binary outcomes (anemia, preterm birth, low birth weight, NICU admission). Effect estimates are reported as adjusted β coefficients or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. All models were adjusted for the covariates listed above.

We included the number of ANC visits and iron-folate adherence as covariates in the primary models, though these may be mediators rather than confounders. To address this, separate mediation analyses ( Figure S2 ) estimated direct and indirect effects through these pathways. The primary adjusted model provides a conservative estimate of the total intervention effect by controlling for potential pathways, while the mediation analysis decomposes direct and indirect effects, offering a more complete understanding of causal mechanisms.

Given the nested structure (women within facilities) and facility-level intervention assignment, we employed mixed-effects models with random intercepts for facilities and included facility-level covariates (size, location, staffing, laboratory availability) as fixed effects. The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) quantified the between-facility variance. We acknowledge that with only 12 facilities, cluster-level adjustment may be underpowered; this limitation is discussed in the Limitations section.

Effect modification was tested by baseline anemia, parity, and education using interaction terms. Model fit was assessed via the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (logistic) and residual diagnostics (linear). Multicollinearity was evaluated using variance inflation factors (VIF < 5 considered acceptable).

To address potential confounding from the non-randomized allocation, we performed propensity score matching as a key sensitivity analysis. 15 Detailed specifications of the propensity score model, matching algorithm, balance diagnostics, and results in the matched sample are provided in File S11 .

Missing data were < 8% for all variables except adherence (12%). Missingness was assumed to be at random. We performed complete-case analysis for primary analyses and multiple imputation by chained equations (m = 20) as a sensitivity analysis. The pattern of missingness was examined using logistic regression with a missingness indicator.

Difference-in-Differences (DID) analysis: To strengthen causal inference, we conducted a quasi-experimental DID analysis comparing hemoglobin trajectories between groups. This approach controls for time-invariant confounders and common time trends by comparing changes over time between the intervention and control groups. The parallel trends assumption was assessed using monthly hemoglobin measurements during the baseline period; the assumption was considered satisfied if the pre-intervention trend difference was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Full DID specifications, including model details, parallel trends testing, event study analysis, and robustness checks, are documented in File S2 .

To assess the robustness of our primary findings against potential unmeasured confounding, we calculated E-values for the primary outcome (follow-up hemoglobin) using the method proposed by VanderWeele and Ding (2017). 16 The E-value represents the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the intervention and the outcome to explain away the observed effect, conditional on measured covariates. An E-value substantially larger than typical effect sizes for known confounders strengthens causal inference in observational studies.

All analyses were conducted using R version 4.3.1 and SPSS version 28.0. The complete R script for primary analyses, including multivariable regression, propensity score matching, and mediation analysis, is provided in File S13 . A comprehensive data dictionary with variable definitions, measurement details, and data quality indicators is available in File S14 .

This study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from the Al-Dhalea Health Office Ethics Committee (DHL-REC/2024/112; January–December 2025). Ethics documents are available from the corresponding author upon request (not included in supplementary materials per journal policy).

All participants provided written informed consent; for adolescents (15–17 years), parental consent and adolescent assent were obtained. Consent forms (English: File S3 ; Arabic: available upon request) were read aloud in the local dialect with pictorial aids to ensure comprehension, given the high illiteracy rates.

Confidentiality was maintained through anonymization, password-protected storage, and restricted access. No enrollment incentives were offered; transport reimbursement ($5 per visit) was provided to offset access costs. Data collectors and nurses received ethics training ( File S4 ).

Vulnerable population protections: Additional measures included: (1) separation of enrollment from care to minimize coercion; (2) oral consent with comprehension verification and witnesses for illiterate participants; (3) age-appropriate language for adolescent assent; (4) ethics-reviewed transport reimbursement to avoid undue influence; and (5) safety protocols (home visits only when secure, phone follow-ups during insecurity, and satellite phones for emergency communication).

This study was designed and reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cohort studies. A completed STROBE checklist is provided in File S1 .

Between January and June 2025, 532 pregnant women were assessed for eligibility at 12 primary healthcare facilities in Al-Dhalea Governorate. Of these, 450 met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled ( Figure 1 ). Complete follow-up until delivery was achieved for 435 participants (96.7%), with 15 lost to follow-up due to displacement or transfer, showing no differential attrition between groups (p = 0.42).

Baseline characteristics of the 450 participants are presented in Table 1 . The cohort comprised 224 women in the nurse-led ANC group and 226 in the routine ANC group. The groups were generally comparable in age, residence, and parity. However, women in the nurse-led group had modest but statistically significant advantages at baseline: higher educational attainment (14.3% vs 7.1% with higher education, p = 0.03), higher hemoglobin levels (10.2 ± 0.9 g/dL vs 9.9 ± 1.0 g/dL, p = 0.002), and more ANC visits (mean 5.8 vs 4.3 visits, p < 0.001). All these variables were included as covariates in adjusted analyses to address potential confounding.

Nurse-led ANC was associated with a mean increase of 1.05 g/dL in follow-up hemoglobin (95% CI: 0.82–1.28, p < 0.001) and lower odds of anemia at follow-up (adjusted OR = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.21–0.48, p < 0.001). Using 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement (caliper = 0.2), we achieved balanced groups (n = 200 per group). In this matched sample, nurse-led ANC remained associated with higher follow-up hemoglobin (adjusted β = 1.02 g/dL, 95% CI: 0.75–1.29, p < 0.001) and lower odds of anemia (adjusted OR = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.23–0.53, p < 0.001). Complete methodology and balance tables are shown in File S11 .

Using mixed-effects models with facility as a random intercept, the results remained consistent: adjusted β for hemoglobin = +1.01 g/dL (95% CI: 0.78–1.24, p < 0.001), and adjusted OR for anemia = 0.34 (95% CI: 0.22–0.51, p < 0.001). The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.08, indicating that 8% of the variance in hemoglobin outcomes was attributable to between-facility differences.

For the primary hemoglobin effect (β = 1.05 g/dL; partial correlation ≈ 0.35), the E-value was 2.41. For the lower 95% CI bound (β = 0.82 g/dL), the E-value was 1.98. These exceed the effect sizes of most known maternal health confounders (eg, baseline anemia, education, parity), suggesting that unmeasured confounding is unlikely to fully account for the observed benefit.

Birth outcomes are presented in Table 3 . Nurse-led ANC was associated with significantly reduced odds of low birth weight (<2500 g; adjusted OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.94, p = 0.02). A trend toward reduced preterm birth was observed but did not reach statistical significance (adjusted OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.45–1.02, p = 0.06). No significant differences were found for NICU admission or caesarean delivery. A comprehensive visual summary of all adjusted associations is provided in the forest plot ( Figure 3 ).

Implementation fidelity was assessed across three domains: protocol adherence, barriers encountered, and severe anemia management (Hb < 7 g/dL). As shown in Table 4 , protocol adherence exceeded 83% across all domains. Despite contextual barriers (supply disruptions, power outages, and security constraints), nurses successfully maintained core protocol elements. Critically, all eight cases of severe anemia were identified and referred, with 87.5% successfully reaching higher-level care, demonstrating clinical leadership in emergency recognition and referral coordination.

Comparable process indicators from routine ANC facilities were not systematically collected, as the routine care model did not implement standardized documentation of these indicators. This represents a limitation in our ability to fully compare implementation fidelity between groups.

The effect of nurse-led ANC on anemia reduction varied significantly by baseline anemia status (p for interaction = 0.01; Table 5 ). The intervention was more beneficial among anemic women at baseline (adjusted OR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.16–0.39) compared to non-anemic women (adjusted OR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.32–2.05). Consistent benefits were observed across parity and education subgroups, with slightly larger effect sizes among women with no formal education. Additional subgroup analyses are presented in Figure S1 . Full sensitivity analysis results are provided in Table S1 .

Pathway analysis revealed that the beneficial effect of nurse-led ANC on hemoglobin levels was partially mediated by two key mechanisms: an increased number of ANC visits (accounting for 28% of the total effect) and improved adherence to iron-folate supplementation (accounting for 19%). The direct effect of the intervention remained substantial and significant (53% of the total effect, p < 0.001). Complete mediation analysis results are available in Figure S2 .

Multiple sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of our primary findings. A per-protocol analysis excluding participants with fewer than three ANC visits yielded similar results (adjusted β for Hb = +1.08 g/dL, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32). Propensity score matching (1:1 matching, n = 200 per group) produced comparable effect estimates (adjusted OR for anaemia = 0.35, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.53). Complete-case analysis and multiple imputation approaches yielded consistent results. A comprehensive comparison of effect estimates across all analytical approaches is presented in Table 6 . Detailed sensitivity analysis results are provided in Table S1 .

All sensitivity analyses yielded results consistent with primary findings, supporting the robustness of our conclusions.

No adverse events related to the nurse-led intervention were reported. The standardized adverse event reporting form and the 72-hour reporting protocol to the ethics committee are detailed in File S7 . Process indicators showed significantly better performance in the nurse-led group: adherence to iron-folate supplementation was 78.3% versus 51.8% (p < 0.001), and patient satisfaction scores were higher (mean 8.7/10 vs 6.2/10, p < 0.001). The distribution of birth weights by ANC type is illustrated in Figure S3 .

All regression models met the assumptions of linearity, homoscedasticity, and the absence of influential outliers. Variance inflation factors ranged from 1.1 to 2.7, indicating no concerning multicollinearity. Hosmer-Lemeshow tests for logistic models showed adequate fit (all p-values > 0.20). Complete regression diagnostics and model specifications are detailed in Table S2 , with reproducible analysis code in File S13 .

The nurse-led intervention cost approximately $18 per woman (95% UI: $14–$24), averting an estimated 0.042 DALYs per woman (0.031–0.053), primarily from reduced anemia and low birth weight. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) was estimated at $429 per DALY averted (95% UI: $298–$612), falling below the WHO cost-effectiveness threshold (1×GDP per capita for Yemen = $650). This estimate includes direct intervention costs (training, supplies, equipment amortization, supervision, and data collection) and represents the base case analysis. The point estimate before applying the conservative 3% annual discount rate and accounting for uncertainty was $335 ( File S15 ). The base case estimate of $429 is used in the main manuscript as it represents a more comprehensive and conservative assessment of cost-effectiveness. In probabilistic sensitivity analysis, the ICER remained below the threshold in 89% of simulations. Detailed cost breakdowns, DALY calculations, and probabilistic sensitivity analysis are available in File S15 . This preliminary analysis is based on modeled estimates and should be interpreted with caution pending prospective validation with comprehensive cost data.

The DID estimator (β 3 ) for hemoglobin change was +1.12 g/dL (95% CI: 0.86 to 1.38, p < 0.001), consistent with the primary findings. The parallel trends assumption was satisfied (pre-intervention trend difference: −0.08 g/dL/month, p = 0.42). This quasi-experimental approach provides supportive evidence for intervention effects beyond observational associations. Full DID methodology, including parallel trends validation and heterogeneity assessment, is reported in File S2 .

In this prospective cohort study from conflict-affected Yemen, we found that nurse-led antenatal care was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in maternal hemoglobin levels, substantially reduced odds of anemia at follow-up, and a decreased likelihood of low birth weight. These findings persisted after rigorous adjustment for demographic, obstetric, and health service covariates and demonstrated robustness across multiple sensitivity analyses ( Table S1 ). Our study makes several contributions to the literature on task-shifting and maternal health in humanitarian settings. The study was designed and reported following STROBE guidelines ( File S1 ).

From a global health systems perspective, our findings suggest that task-shifting may be moving from a normative recommendation toward an outcome-informed strategy. While previous studies have primarily assessed task-shifting through service coverage or process indicators, this study provides evidence that structured nurse-led antenatal care can be associated with measurable biological and neonatal benefits, even in severely constrained, conflict-affected health systems.

The prevalence of anaemia at follow-up in the routine ANC group (67.8%) is consistent with previously reported figures from Yemen 4 and aligns with findings from other humanitarian settings. For example, a recent study among pregnant refugee women in Uganda reported an anaemia prevalence of 52.6%, with low education and food insecurity identified as significant contributors. 5 The substantially lower prevalence observed in our nurse-led ANC group (38.2%) suggests that structured, protocol-driven care may mitigate some of these contextual risk factors, even in resource-constrained and conflict-affected environments. This finding reinforces the potential of nurse-led models to deliver meaningful health gains where physician availability is structurally constrained.

Our primary finding—that nurse-led ANC increased hemoglobin by 1.05 g/dL compared to routine care—represents a substantial effect. This gain exceeds the significant hemoglobin improvement established for standard iron supplementation, a core component of ANC, as confirmed by a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. 17 Our effect size of 1.05 g/dL suggests particular relevance in conflict contexts where baseline care quality is severely compromised. The 68% reduction in anemia odds (adjusted OR 0.32) similarly surpasses reductions reported in meta-analyses of iron supplementation programs alone (typically a 30–50% reduction), 18 indicating that structured, nurse-delivered care packages may yield synergistic benefits beyond micronutrient provision.

Our findings extend beyond clinical outcomes to suggest how task-shifting may contribute to core health system functions in conflict settings. The nurse-led model was associated with improvements in service delivery (structured protocols), health workforce optimization (role redistribution), and information systems (systematic monitoring)—key building blocks of resilient health systems. 19 This evidence may be particularly relevant given global efforts to rebuild health systems in post-conflict transitions and humanitarian responses.

The observed reduction in low birth weight (38% lower odds) aligns with biological plausibility: improved maternal hemoglobin enhances oxygen delivery to the fetus, supporting optimal growth. 20 Previous studies have established the hemoglobin–birth weight relationship, 21 and our study suggests that task-shifting interventions may influence this pathway even in conflict settings. The non-significant trend toward reduced preterm birth (32% lower odds, p = 0.06) may reflect insufficient power for this less frequent outcome or, alternatively, that hemoglobin improvements primarily affect fetal growth rather than gestational duration.

Beyond Yemen-specific findings, this study offers a potential Fragility-Adapted Care (FAC) framework with three core components: (1) task consolidation (structured protocols for existing nurses), (2) supply decoupling (minimal essential commodities), and (3) resilience anchoring (community-integrated follow-up). These components are intended to be context-agnostic and potentially applicable across fragility gradients. The intervention’s effect heterogeneity analysis ( File S11 ) showed consistent benefits regardless of facility size or remoteness, suggesting broader applicability in similar resource-constrained, conflict-affected settings in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, though further validation in diverse contexts is warranted.

Notably, food insecurity and poor education were found to be important risk factors for anemia by Bongomin et al (2025), 5 and these characteristics are similarly common in our research sample ( Table 1 ). This implies that groups with high levels of social vulnerability, where organized education and nutritional counseling can have the biggest effects, may benefit most from nurse-led ANC.

Importantly, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of “second-best” care delivered in the absence of physicians. Rather, they demonstrate that nurse-led antenatal care represents a resilient and clinically effective model capable of sustaining essential maternal services under conditions of health system collapse. In conflict-affected settings where physician availability is structurally constrained, task-shifting to trained nurses is not merely a temporary coping strategy but a viable pathway to preserving care continuity and improving biological outcomes. The observed improvements in maternal hemoglobin levels and reductions in low birth weight suggest that appropriately supported nurse-led models can deliver meaningful health gains, even in the most resource-constrained and unstable environments. This has direct implications for policy and practice, supporting the intentional scale-up of nurse-led antenatal care as a core component of health system adaptation and resilience in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

Our mediation analysis suggests that approximately half of the total effect on hemoglobin was attributable to increased ANC visit frequency and improved iron-folate adherence. This aligns with implementation science frameworks emphasizing that successful interventions in fragile settings often work through improving fundamental care delivery processes. 22 The remaining direct effect (53%) likely captures the added value of the structured, protocol-driven quality of the nurse-led model. This includes components that are difficult to measure quantitatively but are crucial for outcomes, such as improved quality of health education, more time for patient counseling, better complication detection through systematic checklists, and enhanced psychosocial support—elements often missing in fragmented, crisis-affected systems. 23 Future qualitative work should explore these experiential aspects of care. Our structured assessment of patient satisfaction, reported with systematic documentation of implementation fidelity and process indicators following the COREQ framework ( File S10 ), provides a foundation for such deeper exploration. Notably, no formal qualitative interviews or focus groups were conducted; the COREQ checklist was adapted to document patient-reported experience measures and implementation fidelity indicators.

The intervention demonstrated a significantly greater benefit among women who were anaemic at baseline (a 75% reduction in anaemia odds vs a non-significant effect among non-anaemic women). This is a key finding for policy and practice, as it indicates that the enhanced nurse-led model is particularly effective for the highest-risk group. In resource-constrained conflict settings, this supports a prioritization strategy where targeting structured ANC towards women identified with anaemia early in pregnancy could maximize the population-level impact and efficiency of the intervention.

These findings offer several considerations for global health policymakers and humanitarian practitioners. First, they provide empirical support for WHO’s task-shifting recommendations in emergencies, 24 complementing expert opinion with outcome-based evidence. In Yemen, where 60% lack access to physicians, 4 strategic investments in nursing capacity represent a viable health system strengthening strategy.

Second, the intervention demonstrates that simple, protocol-driven approaches improve care quality despite severe constraints. The model builds on the existing workforce, avoiding the costly recruitment of new cadres. The reduction in low birth weight may generate long-term cost savings by averting complications. 25

Third, the greater benefit among anemic women at baseline (75% reduction in anemia odds) supports targeting enhanced nurse-led care toward high-risk women identified early in pregnancy, maximizing efficiency in resource-limited settings.

At an estimated $429 per DALY averted (preliminary analysis), this intervention may represent favorable economic value for humanitarian health investment. However, this estimate should be interpreted with caution due to the preliminary nature of the cost analysis and the omission of important cost components (supervision, monitoring, transport, equipment maintenance, administration, and supply chain management). Further prospective cost-effectiveness analysis is needed to confirm these findings.

The nurse-led approach showed traits that may be categorized as “emergent leadership” in health systems that are vulnerable. First, the approach did not use formal leadership titles; instead, leadership in this setting seemed to come from managing obstacles and putting defined norms into place. Second, three aspects of leadership-related activity were noted: community leadership (maintaining patient engagement and offering health education), administrative leadership (organizing follow-up schedules and referral pathways), and clinical leadership (independent protocol-driven anemia management). Despite not being explicitly quantified as leadership results, these characteristics offer a potentially helpful framework for humanitarian training programs. Third, while this should be read cautiously, the preliminary cost-effectiveness assessment indicates that investing in nursing capacity may be an effective use of limited resources in conflict contexts.

The implementation fidelity data ( Table 4 ) reveal three mechanisms. First, protocol adherence exceeded 83% despite contextual instability; written algorithms reduced cognitive load and enabled consistent care when supervision was intermittent. Second, nurses actively managed barriers: they maintained buffer stocks for supply disruptions, rescheduled testing during power outages, and conducted phone follow-ups during road closures. Third, all eight women with Hb < 7 g/dL were correctly identified and referred, with 87.5% reaching higher-level care—demonstrating clinical leadership autonomy in emergency recognition and referral coordination despite the absence of physicians.

Key strengths include: (1) prospective design in an active conflict zone with a 96.7% follow-up rate, providing rare outcome-level evidence; (2) rigorous confounding adjustment using DAG-informed covariate selection and comprehensive sensitivity analyses (propensity score matching, multiple imputation, inverse probability weighting; File S11 ; Table 6 ); (3) standardized HemoCue ® hemoglobin measurement; (4) detailed contextual profile ( File S12 ) and de-identified dataset for reproducibility; (5) ROBINS-I framework 26 for transparent bias assessment; (6) quasi-experimental difference-in-differences analysis ( File S2 ) strengthening causal inference; (7) preliminary cost-effectiveness analysis ($429/DALY; File S15); and (8) fully reproducible code ( File S13 ) and data documentation ( File S14 ).

Non-randomized allocation by facility capacity introduces selection bias. Nurse-led facilities had better baseline staffing, laboratory function, and participant characteristics (higher hemoglobin, education, ANC visits). Despite multivariable adjustment, propensity score matching ( File S11 ), and mixed-effects modeling, unmeasured facility-level factors (supervision, supplies, referral systems) may explain some observed effects rather than the protocol itself. DID analysis ( File S2 ) partially addresses time-invariant differences but does not fully resolve confounding. Findings should be interpreted as associations, not causal effects.

Unmeasured factors (diet, food security, infections, hemoglobinopathies) may influence outcomes. An E-value of 2.41 suggests that confounding would need to be strong to fully explain the effects, but residual confounding remains possible.

Only two time points limit parallel trends testing. While statistically significant (p = 0.42), divergence in unmeasured trends during the intervention cannot be ruled out. DID results are supportive, not definitive causal proof.

Our findings are consistent with evidence from other humanitarian settings, such as a recent study among pregnant refugee women in Uganda that reported an anemia prevalence of 52.6%. 5 However, the generalizability of our results should be considered with caution. The intervention was implemented in a single governorate under specific organizational, geographical, and humanitarian conditions. Contextual factors—including workforce availability, local governance, infrastructure, security conditions, and resource allocation—may substantially influence the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach elsewhere. Further validation studies in diverse humanitarian settings are needed to confirm the transferability of the nurse-led ANC model.

Based on modeled estimates, missing costs (supervision, nurse time, transport, maintenance, administration, supply chain) were identified. The ICER of $ 429/DALY (95% UI: $ 298–$ 612) requires cautious interpretation and prospective validation ( File S15 ).

Despite limitations, the findings were robust across multiple sensitivity analyses ( Tables 6 and S1 ), with consistent estimates across multivariable regression, propensity score matching, multiple imputation, inverse probability weighting, mixed-effects modeling, and DID.

(1) cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge designs; (2) formal cost-effectiveness analysis with comprehensive cost data; (3) qualitative studies of patient experiences; (4) component contribution analysis; (5) geographical and social vulnerability variation; and (6) health literacy as an effect modifier.

Future studies should employ cluster-randomized designs to establish causality definitively, incorporate economic evaluations to assess cost-effectiveness, and examine longer-term child development outcomes. Qualitative research exploring women’s experiences with nurse-led care in conservative, conflict-affected communities would complement our quantitative findings. Additionally, research is needed on optimal implementation strategies—including training duration, supervision models, and supply chain adaptations—for maximum sustainability in volatile environments.

In conflict-affected Yemen, structured nurse-led antenatal care was associated with improved maternal hemoglobin levels, reduced anemia prevalence, and decreased low birth weight. A preliminary economic estimate suggested a favorable value of $429 per DALY averted, though this requires prospective validation. These findings suggest that task-shifting to nurses may represent a feasible and effective strategy for maintaining essential maternal health services in humanitarian crises.

However, there are a few crucial disclaimers to take into account. These results should be viewed as associations rather than causal effects due to the non-randomized design, facility-level confounding, and baseline differences between groups. Although our findings demonstrate the potential of nurse-led models, they do not provide conclusive proof that the observed improvements were solely the result of nurse-led care. Although the model exhibits traits that are compatible with adaptive leadership, leadership itself was not quantified.

Humanitarian health actors may want to think about whether organized nurse-led care may be a useful part of maternal health service delivery in active conflict contexts, since this evidence may have policy implications. To determine causality and assess the relative contributions of various model components, we highly advise additional testing of this model using more stringent designs, ideally cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge trials. Although implementation research is required to confirm this, the intervention’s relative simplicity and favorable preliminary cost-effectiveness estimates suggest potential for scalability.

By using standardized nursing data and examining whether nurse-led models can reduce disparities in maternal healthcare delivery across various geographic settings and levels of social vulnerability, future research should investigate the processes behind these findings.

Fragile and conflict-affected settings face profound health system disruptions, including workforce shortages, fragmented service delivery, and reduced access to essential maternal health services. Task-shifting from physicians to nurses has been promoted as a pragmatic strategy to sustain service delivery; yet, empirical evidence on its impact on biological and neonatal outcomes in active conflict settings remains scarce. The critical question is whether nurse-led care models can function as an adaptive strategy that preserves outcomes during health system collapse.

In Al-Dhalea Governorate, where this study was conducted, access to antenatal care (ANC) is severely constrained. Only 45% of health facilities are fully functional, with physician-to-population ratios of 1:15,000 (far below WHO recommendations) and 2 to 3 nurses per facility serving 5,000 to 10,000 people. Iron-folate supply disruptions occur for 3 to 4 months annually, and referral pathways are often obstructed by road closures. The baseline prevalence of anemia among pregnant women is estimated at 70% to 75%, with food insecurity affecting more than 60% of households.

Maternal anemia remains a critical global challenge, disproportionately affecting low-resource and conflict-affected settings. 1 Defined as hemoglobin levels < 11 g/dL during pregnancy, anemia contributes to preterm birth, low birth weight, and maternal mortality. 2 In humanitarian crises, health systems face compounded challenges: infrastructure collapse, workforce shortages, supply chain disruptions, and displacement. 3 Yemen exemplifies this fragility, with over a decade of conflict leaving an estimated 65% of pregnant women anemic and maternal mortality rates having tripled since 2015. 4 The burden of maternal anemia is not confined to Yemen; recent evidence from other humanitarian settings, such as refugee populations in Uganda, reported an anemia prevalence of 52.6% among pregnant women, with low educational attainment and food insecurity identified as key determinants. 5

Strengthening nurse-delivered ANC through structured protocols, systematic screening, and algorithm-based management has emerged as an essential adaptation. 6 ANC is a promising domain for optimization, given its preventive, protocol-driven nature. 7 While task-shifting has shown effectiveness in HIV and immunization programs, 8 , 9 its impact on maternal anemia and birth outcomes in active conflict settings remains inadequately documented. Previous studies in stable settings suggest that nurse-led interventions can improve ANC attendance and maternal knowledge, 10 but evidence from conflict zones is scarce, with most studies focusing on process rather than biological outcomes. 11 There is still little data on the efficacy of organized, nurse-led treatments in enhancing biological and newborn outcomes in active conflict areas, despite recent research showing the high prevalence of anemia in humanitarian contexts and identifying related risk factors. 5 Instead than focusing on clinical outcomes, the majority of previous research has examined procedural indicators like attendance rates. Therefore, strong prospective evidence is essential for guiding measures to enhance the health system in fragile environments.

We conceptualize nurse-led ANC as de facto nursing leadership that emerges when physicians are structurally constrained. This informal leadership manifests across three dimensions: (1) clinical leadership—independent, protocol-driven anemia management; (2) administrative leadership—coordinating follow-up and referrals despite supply disruptions; and (3) community leadership—sustaining health education and patient engagement. We hypothesize that these dimensions, operationalized through structured protocols, may translate into measurable biological improvements. This framework guides interpretation while acknowledging that leadership was not directly measured but inferred from implementation fidelity.

The theoretical foundation derives from the chronic care model adapted to humanitarian contexts, emphasizing structured follow-up, patient education, and protocol-based management. 12 Complex confounders in fragile environments, such as supply interruptions, security limitations, and varied training, are frequently overlooked in existing studies. 11 New research indicates that health literacy may interact with nursing complexity to influence patient outcomes 13 and that nursing variables may mediate the relationship between patient clinical complexity and organizational outcomes. 14 Therefore, there is an urgent need for solid prospective research about whether improved nurse-led ANC improves biological and neonatal outcomes in active combat zones.

This study addresses these gaps by evaluating a fragility-adapted intervention in Al-Dhalea, Yemen. Specifically, we aimed to: (1) quantify associations between nurse-led ANC and hemoglobin, anemia, and birth outcomes compared to routine ANC; (2) assess whether structured nurse-led ANC demonstrates characteristics consistent with de facto nursing leadership across clinical, administrative, and community dimensions, as measured by implementation fidelity; and (3) derive a preliminary adaptation framework for health system strengthening in degrading contexts while acknowledging observational evidence limitations.

We conducted a prospective cohort study between January and December 2025 across 12 public primary healthcare facilities in Al-Dhalea Governorate, southern Yemen—a region severely affected by protracted conflict, fragmented health services, recurrent displacement, and chronic shortages of medical personnel and supplies. Facilities were purposively selected to represent typical service delivery in conflict-affected settings, including intermittent laboratory functionality, essential medicine stockouts, and limited referral pathways. A comprehensive contextual profile, including facility characteristics, implementation challenges, and adaptive strategies, is available in File S12 .

The 12 facilities comprised six nurse-led and six routine ANC sites, selected based on (1) trained nurse availability, (2) geographic distribution (urban/rural balance), and (3) protocol implementation capacity. Nurse-led facilities had slightly better baseline staffing (mean 2.2 vs 1.3 ANC nurses per facility) and laboratory functionality (83% vs 50% with functional labs) compared to routine facilities. These differences were addressed through facility-level covariate adjustment and sensitivity analyses and are discussed as a key limitation. Detailed facility-level characteristics (staffing, laboratory functionality, power availability, security access, catchment population) are provided in File S12 .

Pregnant women seeking prenatal care at participating facilities during the recruiting period were included in the study population. To reduce selection bias, all eligible women who visited each institution throughout the recruiting period were asked to take part.

Exclusion criteria were known hemoglobinopathies (eg, sickle cell disease, thalassemia), chronic renal impairment, active tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, or any medical condition requiring specialized obstetric care (eg, cardiac disease, pre-existing diabetes). These exclusions were applied to minimize clinical heterogeneity and reduce confounding by underlying pathologies affecting hemoglobin metabolism or pregnancy outcomes.

Nurse-led enhanced ANC cohort: Women who received structured antenatal care delivered primarily by trained nurses following a standardised care protocol detailed in File S6 . The protocol included systematic haemoglobin screening, algorithm-based anaemia management, regular follow-up visits, nutrition education, and clear referral pathways.

The allocation of participants to nurse-led or routine ANC was determined by facility-level implementation capacity rather than individual randomization. The 12 participating facilities were purposively selected to ensure representation of both care models based on (1) the availability of trained nurses for the enhanced protocol and (2) geographic distribution to include comparable urban/rural settings. Women received the type of ANC available at the facility where they enrolled. To minimize selection bias, all eligible women presenting to each facility during the recruitment period were invited to participate, and baseline characteristics were rigorously measured and adjusted for in the analyses.

The sample size was estimated to detect a clinically meaningful difference in mean hemoglobin concentration between groups. Based on pilot data from similar settings in Yemen, we assumed a mean difference of 0.5 g/dL with a standard deviation of 1.2 g/dL. With α = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power, the required sample size was 91 participants per group. Accounting for a 15% loss to follow-up, we targeted 107 participants per group (214 total). For increased precision and to accommodate subgroup analyses, we recruited 225 participants per group (450 total). Detailed power calculation methodology and assumptions are provided in File S9 .

Data were collected using structured, pre-tested instruments ( File S4 ). At enrollment, trained data collectors (midwives with ≥ 2 years of experience, see File S5 for training details) administered baseline questionnaires capturing socio-demographic characteristics, obstetric history, gestational age, and baseline hemoglobin levels measured using HemoCue ® Hb 301 devices. Follow-up assessments occurred during scheduled ANC visits and at delivery, with hemoglobin remeasured at 32–34 weeks. Birth outcomes were abstracted from facility records or obtained through structured postnatal interviews for community births. All data collectors underwent standardized training ( File S5 ), and data management followed a predefined protocol ( File S8 ). A single quantitative item (scale 1–10) was used to evaluate patient satisfaction as a secondary process measure. The SRQR and COREQ checklists mentioned in the supplemental files apply to the systematic documenting of implementation fidelity and process indicators rather than formal qualitative research components because we did not gather qualitative interview data.

Based on directed acyclic graphs constructed a priori, we distinguished between confounders (variables affecting both exposure and outcome) and mediators (variables on the causal pathway). The following covariates were identified for adjustment in the main models as potential confounders:

The following variables were considered potential mediators rather than confounders and were therefore not included as adjustment variables in the primary models: (1) the number of ANC visits and (2) adherence to iron–folic acid supplementation. These variables were instead analyzed separately in a mediation analysis to quantify the pathways through which the intervention may have operated (see the Mediation Analysis section and Figure S2 ).

Baseline characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics: means (SD) or medians (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies (percentages) for categorical variables. Group differences were assessed using Student’s t -test or Mann–Whitney U -test for continuous variables, and χ 2 or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables.

Multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors estimated the adjusted association between nurse-led ANC and follow-up hemoglobin. Multivariable logistic regression was used for binary outcomes (anemia, preterm birth, low birth weight, NICU admission). Effect estimates are reported as adjusted β coefficients or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. All models were adjusted for the covariates listed above.

We included the number of ANC visits and iron-folate adherence as covariates in the primary models, though these may be mediators rather than confounders. To address this, separate mediation analyses ( Figure S2 ) estimated direct and indirect effects through these pathways. The primary adjusted model provides a conservative estimate of the total intervention effect by controlling for potential pathways, while the mediation analysis decomposes direct and indirect effects, offering a more complete understanding of causal mechanisms.

Given the nested structure (women within facilities) and facility-level intervention assignment, we employed mixed-effects models with random intercepts for facilities and included facility-level covariates (size, location, staffing, laboratory availability) as fixed effects. The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) quantified the between-facility variance. We acknowledge that with only 12 facilities, cluster-level adjustment may be underpowered; this limitation is discussed in the Limitations section.

Effect modification was tested by baseline anemia, parity, and education using interaction terms. Model fit was assessed via the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (logistic) and residual diagnostics (linear). Multicollinearity was evaluated using variance inflation factors (VIF < 5 considered acceptable).

To address potential confounding from the non-randomized allocation, we performed propensity score matching as a key sensitivity analysis. 15 Detailed specifications of the propensity score model, matching algorithm, balance diagnostics, and results in the matched sample are provided in File S11 .

Missing data were < 8% for all variables except adherence (12%). Missingness was assumed to be at random. We performed complete-case analysis for primary analyses and multiple imputation by chained equations (m = 20) as a sensitivity analysis. The pattern of missingness was examined using logistic regression with a missingness indicator.

Difference-in-Differences (DID) analysis: To strengthen causal inference, we conducted a quasi-experimental DID analysis comparing hemoglobin trajectories between groups. This approach controls for time-invariant confounders and common time trends by comparing changes over time between the intervention and control groups. The parallel trends assumption was assessed using monthly hemoglobin measurements during the baseline period; the assumption was considered satisfied if the pre-intervention trend difference was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Full DID specifications, including model details, parallel trends testing, event study analysis, and robustness checks, are documented in File S2 .

To assess the robustness of our primary findings against potential unmeasured confounding, we calculated E-values for the primary outcome (follow-up hemoglobin) using the method proposed by VanderWeele and Ding (2017). 16 The E-value represents the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the intervention and the outcome to explain away the observed effect, conditional on measured covariates. An E-value substantially larger than typical effect sizes for known confounders strengthens causal inference in observational studies.

All analyses were conducted using R version 4.3.1 and SPSS version 28.0. The complete R script for primary analyses, including multivariable regression, propensity score matching, and mediation analysis, is provided in File S13 . A comprehensive data dictionary with variable definitions, measurement details, and data quality indicators is available in File S14 .

This study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from the Al-Dhalea Health Office Ethics Committee (DHL-REC/2024/112; January–December 2025). Ethics documents are available from the corresponding author upon request (not included in supplementary materials per journal policy).

All participants provided written informed consent; for adolescents (15–17 years), parental consent and adolescent assent were obtained. Consent forms (English: File S3 ; Arabic: available upon request) were read aloud in the local dialect with pictorial aids to ensure comprehension, given the high illiteracy rates.

Confidentiality was maintained through anonymization, password-protected storage, and restricted access. No enrollment incentives were offered; transport reimbursement ($5 per visit) was provided to offset access costs. Data collectors and nurses received ethics training ( File S4 ).

Vulnerable population protections: Additional measures included: (1) separation of enrollment from care to minimize coercion; (2) oral consent with comprehension verification and witnesses for illiterate participants; (3) age-appropriate language for adolescent assent; (4) ethics-reviewed transport reimbursement to avoid undue influence; and (5) safety protocols (home visits only when secure, phone follow-ups during insecurity, and satellite phones for emergency communication).

This study was designed and reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cohort studies. A completed STROBE checklist is provided in File S1 .

Between January and June 2025, 532 pregnant women were assessed for eligibility at 12 primary healthcare facilities in Al-Dhalea Governorate. Of these, 450 met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled ( Figure 1 ). Complete follow-up until delivery was achieved for 435 participants (96.7%), with 15 lost to follow-up due to displacement or transfer, showing no differential attrition between groups (p = 0.42).

Baseline characteristics of the 450 participants are presented in Table 1 . The cohort comprised 224 women in the nurse-led ANC group and 226 in the routine ANC group. The groups were generally comparable in age, residence, and parity. However, women in the nurse-led group had modest but statistically significant advantages at baseline: higher educational attainment (14.3% vs 7.1% with higher education, p = 0.03), higher hemoglobin levels (10.2 ± 0.9 g/dL vs 9.9 ± 1.0 g/dL, p = 0.002), and more ANC visits (mean 5.8 vs 4.3 visits, p < 0.001). All these variables were included as covariates in adjusted analyses to address potential confounding.

Using mixed-effects models with facility as a random intercept, the results remained consistent: adjusted β for hemoglobin = +1.01 g/dL (95% CI: 0.78–1.24, p < 0.001), and adjusted OR for anemia = 0.34 (95% CI: 0.22–0.51, p < 0.001). The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.08, indicating that 8% of the variance in hemoglobin outcomes was attributable to between-facility differences.

For the primary hemoglobin effect (β = 1.05 g/dL; partial correlation ≈ 0.35), the E-value was 2.41. For the lower 95% CI bound (β = 0.82 g/dL), the E-value was 1.98. These exceed the effect sizes of most known maternal health confounders (eg, baseline anemia, education, parity), suggesting that unmeasured confounding is unlikely to fully account for the observed benefit.

Birth outcomes are presented in Table 3 . Nurse-led ANC was associated with significantly reduced odds of low birth weight (<2500 g; adjusted OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.94, p = 0.02). A trend toward reduced preterm birth was observed but did not reach statistical significance (adjusted OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.45–1.02, p = 0.06). No significant differences were found for NICU admission or caesarean delivery. A comprehensive visual summary of all adjusted associations is provided in the forest plot ( Figure 3 ).

( B ) displays the adjusted odds ratios for binary secondary outcomes: anaemia at follow-up (OR = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.21–0.48), preterm birth (OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.45–1.02), low birth weight (OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.94), and NICU admission (OR = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.42–1.19). Implementation fidelity was assessed across three domains: protocol adherence, barriers encountered, and severe anemia management (Hb < 7 g/dL). As shown in Table 4 , protocol adherence exceeded 83% across all domains. Despite contextual barriers (supply disruptions, power outages, and security constraints), nurses successfully maintained core protocol elements. Critically, all eight cases of severe anemia were identified and referred, with 87.5% successfully reaching higher-level care, demonstrating clinical leadership in emergency recognition and referral coordination.

Despite contextual barriers (supply disruptions, power outages, and security constraints), nurses successfully maintained core protocol elements. Critically, all eight cases of severe anemia were identified and referred, with 87.5% successfully reaching higher-level care—demonstrating clinical leadership in emergency recognition and referral coordination. Comparable process indicators from routine ANC facilities were not systematically collected, as the routine care model did not implement standardized documentation of these indicators. This represents a limitation in our ability to fully compare implementation fidelity between groups.

The effect of nurse-led ANC on anemia reduction varied significantly by baseline anemia status (p for interaction = 0.01; Table 5 ). The intervention was more beneficial among anemic women at baseline (adjusted OR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.16–0.39) compared to non-anemic women (adjusted OR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.32–2.05). Consistent benefits were observed across parity and education subgroups, with slightly larger effect sizes among women with no formal education. Additional subgroup analyses are presented in Figure S1 . Full sensitivity analysis results are provided in Table S1 .

Pathway analysis revealed that the beneficial effect of nurse-led ANC on hemoglobin levels was partially mediated by two key mechanisms: an increased number of ANC visits (accounting for 28% of the total effect) and improved adherence to iron-folate supplementation (accounting for 19%). The direct effect of the intervention remained substantial and significant (53% of the total effect, p < 0.001). Complete mediation analysis results are available in Figure S2 .

Multiple sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of our primary findings. A per-protocol analysis excluding participants with fewer than three ANC visits yielded similar results (adjusted β for Hb = +1.08 g/dL, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32). Propensity score matching (1:1 matching, n = 200 per group) produced comparable effect estimates (adjusted OR for anaemia = 0.35, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.53). Complete-case analysis and multiple imputation approaches yielded consistent results. A comprehensive comparison of effect estimates across all analytical approaches is presented in Table 6 . Detailed sensitivity analysis results are provided in Table S1 .
